title: Washing
hook: water on your face recalls your baptism
tomorrow: why pause before the first bite of breakfast?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: all of today. Prayers, works, joys and sufferings, offered at once. The next stop of the morning is the sink.
screen: `ALL OF TODAY.` → `THE NEXT STOP: THE SINK.`

segments.voice: Cold water on the face: the cheapest reset there is. Two splashes and the fog lifts a little. Some Catholic homes keep a small font of holy water by the front door, and people touch it and make the sign of the cross on the way out. A few drops, a few seconds. So what does a splash of water have to do with baptism, something that happened once, maybe when you were too small to remember?
screen: `TWO SPLASHES, THE FOG LIFTS.` → `A FONT BY THE FRONT DOOR.` → `WHAT DOES IT HAVE TO DO WITH BAPTISM?`

segments.voice: Here's the question underneath: how do you remember something that happened once? Catholics teach that baptism is given once and can't be repeated; it marks a person for good. But it can be remembered, and water is how the tradition remembers it. Paul calls baptism "the laver of regeneration": a washing that makes new. At some Sunday Masses the priest sprinkles the people with water, in memory of baptism. A finger in the holy water at the church door, then the sign of the cross, is the same thing in miniature. So the line baptized again means remembered again, not done twice. And the morning splash can carry the same thought: I was washed once, and I'm still that person. Now a neighbor who washes too. Muslims wash before prayer, a washing called wudu. The Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation: "When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows." And a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih Muslim, pictures sins leaving with the drops of water. Shared: water before standing before God, and the hope of being made clean. One honest difference: wudu is repeated before each prayer and is part of what makes that prayer valid, while a Catholic baptism is given once, and the water afterward is a reminder, not a requirement. Two traditions, both reaching for water as they turn toward God.
screen: `GIVEN ONCE, REMEMBERED OFTEN.` · `THE LAVER OF REGENERATION.` · `WASH YOUR FACES, FOR PRAYER.` · `ALIKE, AND HONESTLY DIFFERENT.` · then, large: `BAPTIZED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, a glass, a sink, a bottle, touch a little of it to your forehead, slowly, and notice how cool it is. Remember one thing about yourself that was true long before today. If you're baptized and you pray, you can make the sign of the cross with wet fingers; if not, let the water simply mark a fresh start.
Washing. Water on the face as a daily reminder of the washing Catholics call baptism.
Your line: baptized again. Not a second baptism, just a fresh remembering, every morning at the sink. Stay well.

chat.meaning: Both turn to water before God. Wudu is repeated before each prayer; holy water recalls a baptism given once. Alike, and honestly different.

Honest difference stated without ranking: wudu repeated before each prayer and required for it; Catholic baptism given once (CCC 1272), with holy water as a reminder (sacramental, CCC 1668), not a requirement. Confirm.

The index carry 'baptized again' is kept exactly; the voice explains it as 'remembered again, not done twice' so no one hears a call to rebaptism. The fork corrects the popular half-truth that Catholics are rebaptized at Easter (they renew baptismal promises).
